A Slope invariant and the A-polynomial of knots

Leo Benard Address: Mathematisches Institut, Georg-August Unversität, Göttingen, Deutschland Email address: leo.benard@mathematik.uni-goettingen.de , Vincent Florens Address: Université de Pau, Pau, France Email address: vincent.florens@univ-pau.fr and Adrien Rodau Address: Université de Pau, France Email address: arodau@univ-pau.fr
Abstract.

The A-polynomial is a knot invariant related to the space of SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) representations of the knot group. In this paper our interests lies in the logarithmic Gauss map of the AA-polynomial. We develop a homological point of view on this function by extending the constructions of Degtyarev, the second author and Lecuona to the setting of non-abelian representations. It defines a rational function on the character variety, which unifies various known invariants such as the change of curves in the Reidemeister function, the modulus of boundary-parabolic representations, the boundary slope of some incompressible surfaces embedded in the exterior of the knot KK or equivalently the slopes of the sides of the Newton polygon of the A-polynomial AKA_{K}. We also present a method to compute this invariant in terms of Alexander matrices and Fox calculus.

2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 57K10, Secondary: 57K14, Tertiary: 57K31

1. Introduction

The set of all representations of a knot group in SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) carries naturally the structure of an algebraic set. This holds also for the characters of these representations, whose set is called the SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})-character variety of the knot. Given a peripheral structure of the knot, the character variety is a plane curve in ℂ∗×ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}\times\mathbb{C}^{*}, whose coordinates MM and LL correspond to the eigenvalues of the meridian mm and the prefered longitude ℓ\ell. The polynomial AK​(L,M)A_{K}(L,M) defining this curve is an invariant of the knot, called the A-polynomial. This invariant contains many interesting informations on the knot; in particular, Boyer and Zhang [4] and Dunfield and Garoufalidis [13] showed that AK=L−1A_{K}=L-1 if and only if KK is trivial.

In this paper, our motivations come, among others, from the following result of Boden:

Theorem 1.1 ([3]).

If the MM-degree degM⁡AK​(L,M)\deg_{M}A_{K}(L,M) of the AA-polynomial is zero, then KK is the trivial knot.

This result motivates the systematic study of the logarithmic Gauss map of the A-polynomial

(1) ML⋅∂MAK​(L,M)∂LAK​(L,M),\frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{\partial_{M}A_{K}(L,M)}{\partial_{L}A_{K}(L,M)},

where ∂M\partial_{M} and ∂L\partial_{L} denote the partial derivatives. By Theorem 1.1, this rational function vanishes identically on {AK=0}\{A_{K}=0\} if and only if KK is trivial.

The logarithmic Gauss map has introduced in [14] by Guelfand, Kapranov and Zelevinsky in order to study some determinantial varieties. Then it has been used for instance by Mikhalkin in [17] for studying the topology of arrangements of real plane curves. In [15], Marché and Guilloux showed it is related with the volume function of the A-polynomial of knots, or more generally of exact polynomials.

Our proposal is to develop a homological point of view on this function, by extending the constructions of Degtyarev, the second author and Lecuona [10, 11] to the setting of non-abelian representations. Let KK be an oriented knot in the 3-sphere S3S^{3} with exterior MKM_{K}. Denote by R⁡(MK)R(M_{K}) and X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}) the SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})-representation and character varieties of the knot KK. We consider representations ρ:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) composed with the adjoint action of SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) on the Lie algebra Ad:SL2⁡(ℂ)→Aut⁡(𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ))\operatorname{Ad}\colon\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})\to\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C})), and show that there is a non-empty Zariski open subset of X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}) such that for all ρ\rho in this subset

  • -

    there is an element vρ∈𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)v_{\rho}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) such that (vρ⊗ℓ,vρ⊗m)(v_{\rho}\otimes\ell,v_{\rho}\otimes m) is a basis of the homology group H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)≃ℂ2H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\simeq\mathbb{C}^{2} with coefficients twisted by Ad∘ρ\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho, and

  • -

    the kernel of the homomorphism induced by the inclusion:

    𝒵⁡(K,Ad∘ρ)=ker⁡(H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)⟶i∗H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ))\mathcal{Z}(K,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)=\ker\left(H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{*}}}{{\longrightarrow}}H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\right)

    is generated by a single vector of the form a​vρ⊗ℓ+b​vρ⊗ma\,v_{\rho}\otimes\ell+b\,v_{\rho}\otimes m for some [b:a]∈ℂℙ1[b:a]\in\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}.

The representations which verify these conditions are called admissible. We define the slope of KK at the admissible representation ρ\rho by

sK​(ρ)=−ba∈ℂ​ℙ1.s_{K}(\rho)=-\frac{b}{a}\in\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}.

We prove that representations which restrict to non-parabolic representations of the boundary ∂MK\partial M_{K} of MKM_{K} are admissible, see Lemma 3.4. If ρ\rho is a boundary-parabolic representation, we define the slope sK​(ρ)s_{K}(\rho) as the modulus of the euclidean structure induced by the restricted representation on π1​(∂MK)\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K}), see Section 3.3. It turns out that these two different definitions fit well and that the following holds.

Proposition 1.2.

The slope depends only on the conjugacy classes of the representations and induces a rational function

sK:X⊂X⁡(MK)⟶ℂ​ℙ1s_{K}:X\subset X(M_{K})\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}

on each irreducible component XX of the character variety.

Note that if the representation is real or unitary, then sKs_{K} takes values in ℝ​ℙ1\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{1} (see Proposition 3.13). For any knot, the function sKs_{K} can be computed by Fox calculus, see Section 3.5. We illustrate the method in the case of the trefoil knot, and further compute the slope of the figure-eight knot.

The following theorem relates sKs_{K} to the original motivation; a precise statement is given in Theorem 4.1.

Theorem 1.3.

The slope function sKs_{K} equals minus the logarithmic Gauss map of the A-polynomial defined in Eq. 1.

We also relate sKs_{K} to the change of curve factor for the Reidemeister torsion. Let 𝕋MK,ℓ​(ρ)\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\ell}(\rho) and 𝕋MK,m​(ρ)\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},m}(\rho) be the Reidemeister torsions according to homology bases induced by the choices of the curves ℓ\ell and mm in ∂MK\partial M_{K}, see Section 3.4.

Proposition 1.4.

The slope coincides with the quotient of Reidemeister torsion:

sK​(ρ)=𝕋MK,ℓ​(ρ)𝕋MK,m​(ρ)s_{K}(\rho)=\frac{\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\ell}(\rho)}{\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},m}(\rho)}

for all ρ\rho such that this formula is well-defined.

Porti had already observed ([18, Corollary 4.9]) that the logarithmic Gauss map of the A-polynomial could be expressed as a ratio of torsions -up to a sign-, and that this ratio of torsions is equal to the modulus of ρ\rho when it is a boundary-parabolic representation ([18, Proposition 4.7]). Our point of view permits to fix and compute the sign ambiguity. Moreover, our results Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 1.3 are more general, since they do not require the Reidemeister torsion to be well-defined, for instance they hold for high dimensional components of the character variety.

Finally, we consider ideal points of the A-polynomial, those are points added at infinity in a compactification of the curve {A(L,M)=0}\{A(L,M)=0\} in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}. In [9], Culler and Shalen constructed incompressible surfaces in MKM_{K} associated to such points. Those surfaces have a non-empty boundary, whose slope is determined by rational number p/qp/q. We prove the following theorem:

Theorem 1.5.

Let y∈ℂ​ℙ2y\in\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{2} be an ideal point of the curve {AK(L,M)=0}\{A_{K}(L,M)=0\}. The value of sKs_{K} at yy equal minus the slope of the Culler–Shalen incompressible surface associated to yy.

This theorem sheds some light on the main theorem of [7], which states that the boundary slopes of the Culler–Shalen surfaces are boundary slopes of the Newton polygon of the A-polynomial. Indeed it is well-known that the logarithmic Gauss map converges at those ideal points to the value of the slope of the corresponding boundary of the Newton polygon.

To conclude this introduction, we mention that the slope invariant can be extended to orthogonal (real) representations of link groups. In this more general setting, the first twisted homology space H1​(∂MK,ρ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\rho) can have an arbitrary dimension higher than 22 and the kernel 𝒵⁡(K,ρ)\mathcal{Z}(K,\rho) might not be a line anymore. However, the space H1​(∂MK,ρ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\rho) carries a natural symplectic structure given by the (twisted) intersection form on ∂MK\partial M_{K}, and 𝒵⁡(K,ρ)\mathcal{Z}(K,\rho) is still a Lagrangian subspace. A construction of Arnold [1] related to the Maslov index allows to construct a generalized slope for this context, lying in S1⊂ℂ∗S^{1}\subset\mathbb{C}^{*}. As it turns out, in the case of a representation ρ:π1​(MK)→SU⁡(2)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SU}(2), both theories coincide via the natural isomorphism ℝ​ℙ1≃S1\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{1}\simeq S^{1}. We postpone rigorous definitions and further study of this invariant to an upcoming article.

Organisation of the paper

In Section 2 we collect basic definitions on character varieties and A-polynomials. In Section 3 we define the slope invariant and we prove Proposition 1.2 and Proposition 1.4. In Section 4 we prove Theorem 1.3. Finally, in Section 5 we prove Theorem 1.5.

2. Representation varieties, character varieties and A-polynomial.

This section is devoted to definitions and properties of representations spaces and character varieties (Section 2.1). We compute the character variety of the group ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} in Section 2.2 and define the A-polynomial of knots in Section 2.3. References for character varieties are [19, 20], the A-polynomial was first defined in [7], see also [6].

2.1. Representation and character varieties

Let Γ\Gamma be a finitely generated group. The representation variety is the affine algebraic set

R⁡(Γ)=Hom​(Γ,SL2⁡(ℂ)).R(\Gamma)=\text{Hom}(\Gamma,\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})).

If Γ\Gamma is generated by nn elements, the representation variety is an algebraic subset of SL2⁡(ℂ)n\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})^{n} given by polynomial relations corresponding to the relations of the group Γ\Gamma. Two different presentations yield naturally isomorphic algebraic sets.

A representation ρ:Γ→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho:\Gamma\rightarrow\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is abelian is ρ⁡(Γ)\rho(\Gamma) is an abelian subgroup of SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). A representation ρ\rho is reducible if there exists a proper subspace of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} invariant under the action of ρ⁡(Γ)\rho(\Gamma). Equivalently, ρ⁡(Γ)\rho(\Gamma) is conjugated to a subgroup of the group of upper-triangular matrices in SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). Abelian representations are reducible, but the converse does not hold. Non-reducible representations are irreducible.

Two representations ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} in R⁡(Γ)R(\Gamma) are equivalent if they have the same trace:

ρ∼ρ′​ if and only if ​Tr⁡ρ⁡(γ)=Tr⁡ρ′​(γ)​, for any ​γ∈Γ.\rho\sim\rho^{\prime}\text{ if and only if }\operatorname{Tr}\rho(\gamma)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho^{\prime}(\gamma)\text{, for any }\gamma\in\Gamma.

The set of equivalence classes of representations coincides with the algebro-geometric quotient of R⁡(Γ)R(\Gamma) by the action of SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) by conjugation. This quotient is usually constructed through invariant theory, and is denoted

X(Γ)=R(Γ)//SL2(ℂ).X(\Gamma)=R(\Gamma)/\!/\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}).

Points of the character variety are called characters. The equivalence class of a representation ρ\rho (the character of OPENρ)\rho) is denoted by χρ:Γ→ℂ\chi_{\rho}:\Gamma\rightarrow\mathbb{C} with χρ​(γ)=Tr⁡(ρ⁡(γ))\chi_{\rho}(\gamma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho(\gamma)) for γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma. If Γ\Gamma is the fundamental group of a manifold WW, we simply write R⁡(W)R(W) and X⁡(W)X(W) for the representation and character varieties of the manifold WW.

Despite being abelian is not a well-defined notion on the character variety, the notion of being reducible makes sense there, since a reducible representation ρ:Γ→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho\colon\Gamma\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) can be characterized by the fact that for any γ,δ∈Γ\gamma,\delta\in\Gamma, the following equality holds (see for instance [9, Lemma 1.2.1]):

(2) Tr⁡ρ⁡(γ​δ​γ−1​δ−1)=2.\operatorname{Tr}\rho\left(\gamma\delta\gamma^{-1}\delta^{-1}\right)=2.

The character variety X⁡(Γ)X(\Gamma) can be decomposed as

X⁡(Γ)=Xirr​(Γ)∪Xred​(Γ),X(\Gamma)=X^{\text{irr}}(\Gamma)\cup X^{\text{red}}(\Gamma),

where Xred​(Γ)X^{\text{red}}(\Gamma) is the set of reducible characters, and its complement Xirr​(Γ)X^{\text{irr}}(\Gamma) is the set of irreducible characters. Eq. 2 implies that Xred​(Γ)X^{\text{red}}(\Gamma) is a Zariski closed subset of X⁡(Γ)X(\Gamma).

An algebraic set is reducible if it can be written as a union of two proper algebraic subset, else it is irreducible. An irreducible component of an algebraic set is a maximal irreducible algebraic subset.

Remark 2.1.

Despite R⁡(Γ)R(\Gamma) or X⁡(Γ)X(\Gamma) are called varieties, they are not quite algebraic varieties in general: they are actually reducible, and might not be reduced as schemes (some points or subspaces might have multiplicity). On the other hand, any irreducible component is irreducible, and in particular reduced, by definition.

Two representations ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} are conjugate if there exists a matrix M∈SL2⁡(ℂ)M\in\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) such that ρ⁡(γ)=M​ρ′​(γ)​M−1\rho(\gamma)=M\rho^{\prime}(\gamma)M^{-1} for every γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma. Two conjugate representations define the same character; the converse is false in general, but true for elements of Xirr​(Γ)X^{\text{irr}}(\Gamma). More precisely, the following holds.

Proposition 2.2.

[9, Proposition 1.5.2] If ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} are two representations Γ→SL2⁡(ℂ)\Gamma\lx@nobreakspace\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) with ρ\rho irreducible and χρ=χρ′\chi_{\rho}=\chi_{\rho^{\prime}}, then ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} are conjugate (and ρ′\rho^{\prime} is irreducible as well).

Two non-conjugate representations having the same character in X⁡(Γ)X(\Gamma) must be reducible. If Γ\Gamma is a knot group, Burde and De Rham [5, 12] showed that the set of characters containing non-conjugate representations is finite.

2.2. The character variety of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2}

We describe explicitly the character variety of a 2-torus S1×S1S^{1}\times S^{1}. Pick a basis m,ℓm,\ell of π1​(S1×S1)=ℤ2\pi_{1}(S^{1}\times S^{1})=\mathbb{Z}^{2}. Any representation in SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is conjugate to a representation ρ\rho given by two commuting matrices of the form

ρ⁡(m)=(M∗0M−1),ρ⁡(ℓ)=(L∗0L−1)\rho(m)=\begin{pmatrix}M&*\\ 0&M^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad\rho(\ell)=\begin{pmatrix}L&*\\ 0&L^{-1}\end{pmatrix}

for M,L∈ℂ∗M,L\in\mathbb{C}^{*}. Each point of the character variety X⁡(S1×S1)X(S^{1}\times S^{1}) has a pre-image in R⁡(S1×S1)R(S^{1}\times S^{1}) of the form

(3) ρ(m)=(M00M−1),ρ(ℓ)=(L00L−1),M,L∈ℂ∗.\rho(m)=\begin{pmatrix}M&0\\ 0&M^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad\rho(\ell)=\begin{pmatrix}L&0\\ 0&L^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad M,L\in\mathbb{C}^{*}.

This pre-image is unique up to the involution σ\sigma of (ℂ∗)2(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2} sending (L,M)(L,M) to (L−1,M−1)(L^{-1},M^{-1}), and X⁡(S1×S1)X(S^{1}\times S^{1}) can be identified with the singular affine complex surface (ℂ∗)2/σ(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}/\sigma. It embedds in ℂ3\mathbb{C}^{3} as the zeros of the polynomial

Δ=x2+y2+z2−x​y​z−4.\Delta=x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xyz-4.

Indeed, the function algebra of X⁡(S1×S1)X(S^{1}\times S^{1}) naturally identifies with the σ\sigma-invariant sub-algebra ℂ⁡[M+M−1,L+L−1]\mathbb{C}[M+M^{-1},L+L^{-1}] of ℂ⁡[L±1,M±1]\mathbb{C}[L^{\pm 1},M^{\pm 1}]. This algebra of invariant functions is isomorphic with ℂ⁡[x,y,z]/(Δ)\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]/(\Delta) through M+M−1↦x,L+L−1↦y,M​L+(M​L)−1↦zM+M^{-1}\mapsto x,L+L^{-1}\mapsto y,ML+(ML)^{-1}\mapsto z. From this description, one sees that the singular locus of X⁡(S1×S1)X(S^{1}\times S^{1}) consists on the four points {(L,M)=(±1,±1)}\{(L,M)=(\pm 1,\pm 1)\}.

2.3. The A-polynomial

Let KK be an oriented knot in S3S^{3} with exterior MKM_{K}. The inclusion ∂MK⊂MK\partial M_{K}\subset M_{K} induces an injective group homomorphism π1​(∂MK)↪π1​(MK)\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K})\hookrightarrow\pi_{1}(M_{K}). Let rr be the restriction map:

r:X⁡(MK)⟶X⁡(∂MK)≃X⁡(S1×S1).r\colon X(M_{K})\longrightarrow X(\partial M_{K})\simeq X(S^{1}\times S^{1}).

For short we denote by ρ∂=r⁡(ρ)\rho_{\partial}=r(\rho) the restriction of ρ\rho to π1​(∂MK)\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K}). By Section 2.2, the choice of the longitude ℓ\ell and the meridian mm induces an identification of X⁡(S1×S1)X(S^{1}\times S^{1}) with a quotient of (ℂ∗)2(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}. The image of rr is a union of points and curves, possibly with multiplicities, see for instance [13, Lemma 2.1]. Discarding the 00-dimensional components, the A-polynomial of KK is the unique polynomial AK​(L,M)A_{K}(L,M) in ℂ⁡[L,M]\mathbb{C}[L,M] whose zero locus in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} is exactly mapped onto the image of rr. Note that AK​(L,M)A_{K}(L,M) is always divisible by L−1L-1. This factor corresponds to the curve of reducible characters. Boyer, Zhang, Dunfield and Garoufalidis have shown the following result.

Theorem 2.3 ([4, 13]).

Let KK be a knot in S3S^{3}. The A-polynomial AK​(L,M)A_{K}(L,M) is equal to (L−1)k(L-1)^{k} for some kk, if and only if KK is the trivial knot (and in this case k=1k=1).

3. The Slope invariant

In this section we define the slope of an admissible representation (Section 3.1), and observe that generic SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C})-representations are admissible. In Section 3.2 we show that the slope is invariant by conjugation of the representation. We prove in Section 3.3 that it yields a rational function on irreducible components of the character variety and that the slope of a real representation is a real number. Then we prove in Section 3.4 that the slope can be written as a quotient of Reidemeister torsions. Finally, in Section 3.5 we describe a procedure to compute the slope with an Alexander matrix.

3.1. Admissible representations

Let VV be a finite dimensional ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space, and ρ:π1​(MK)→GL⁡(V)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{GL}(V) be a representation. The representation extends to a ring homomorphism and VV can be viewed as a right ℤ​[π1​(MK)]\mathbb{Z}[\pi_{1}(M_{K})]-module VρV_{\rho}. The twisted homology H∗​(MK,ρ)H_{*}(M_{K},\rho) is the homology of the complex of ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector spaces:

C∗​(MK,ρ)=Vρ⊗ℤ​[π1​(MK)]C∗​(MK,ℤ⁡[π1​(MK)]).C_{*}(M_{K};\rho)=V_{\rho}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[\pi_{1}(M_{K})]}C_{*}(M_{K};\mathbb{Z}[\pi_{1}(M_{K})]).
Definition 3.1.

A representation ρ:π1​(MK)→GL⁡(V)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{GL}(V) is admissible if it satisfies:

  • -

    there exists vρ∈Vv_{\rho}\in V such that {vρ⊗ℓ,vρ⊗m}\{v_{\rho}\otimes\ell,v_{\rho}\otimes m\} is a basis of H1​(∂MK,Vρ)≃ℂ2H_{1}(\partial M_{K},V_{\rho})\simeq\mathbb{C}^{2},

  • -

    the kernel of the homomorphism induced by inclusion:

    𝒵⁡(K,ρ)=ker⁡(H1​(∂MK,Vρ)⟶i∗H1​(MK,Vρ))\mathcal{Z}(K,\rho)=\ker\left(H_{1}(\partial M_{K},V_{\rho})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{*}}}{{\longrightarrow}}H_{1}(M_{K},V_{\rho})\right)

    has dimension one.

We restrict to representations ρ:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\rightarrow\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). The composition of ρ\rho with the adjoint action Ad\operatorname{Ad} of SL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) on 𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) induces the following representation:

Ad∘ρ:π1​(MK)⟶Aut⁡(𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ))γ⟼(v↦ρ⁡(γ)​v​ρ​(γ)−1).\begin{array}[]{rccc}\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho:&\pi_{1}(M_{K})&\longrightarrow&\mathrm{Aut}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}))\\ &\gamma&\longmapsto&\left(v\mapsto\rho(\gamma)v\rho(\gamma)^{-1}\right).\end{array}
Definition 3.2.

Let ρ:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) be such that Ad∘ρ\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho is admissible. Let a⁡(vρ⊗ℓ)+b⁡(vρ⊗m)a\,(v_{\rho}\otimes\ell)+b\,(v_{\rho}\otimes m) be a generator of 𝒵⁡(K,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(K,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) for some [a:b]∈ℂℙ1[a:b]\in\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} . The slope of the knot KK at the representation ρ\rho is

sK​(ρ)=−ba∈ℂ∪∞.s_{K}(\rho)=-\frac{b}{a}\in\mathbb{C}\cup\infty.
Definition 3.3.

A representation ρ:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is boundary-parabolic if the restriction ρ∂:π1​(∂MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho_{\partial}:\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) is parabolic, that is Tr⁡ρ⁡(γ)=±2\operatorname{Tr}\rho(\gamma)=\pm 2 for any γ∈π1​(∂MK)\gamma\in\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K}).

A boundary-parabolic character is the character of a boundary-parabolic representation.

Lemma 3.4.

Let ρ:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) be a non-parabolic representation. The vector space H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is isomorphic to ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}, and the kernel 𝒵⁡(M,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(M,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is one-dimensional. Moreover, if ρ\rho is not boundary-parabolic, then Ad∘ρ\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho is admissible.

Proof.

The group π1​(MK)\pi_{1}(M_{K}) is generated by pairwise conjugate meridians. If ρ\rho is non-parabolic, then the image of a meridian must differ to ±I2\pm I_{2}, otherwise we would have ρ⁡(π1​(MK))⊂{±I2}\rho(\pi_{1}(M_{K}))\subset\{\pm I_{2}\}.

Consider the complex C∗​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)C_{*}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) with one 00-cell, two 11-cells corresponding to ℓ\ell and mm and one 22-cell. An explicit computation of the homology of shows that the dimension of H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is two. 3.2. The slope of characters

By the following lemma, the slope does not depend on the conjugacy class of an irreducible representation. Combined with Proposition 2.2, it follows that the slope of an irreducible representation depends only on its character.

Lemma 3.6.

Let ρ\rho and ρ′:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℂ)\rho^{\prime}\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) be two irreducible, non boundary-parabolic representations. If ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} are conjugate, then sK​(ρ)=sK​(ρ′)s_{K}(\rho)=s_{K}(\rho^{\prime}).

Proof.

Let AA be a matrix in GL2⁡(ℂ)\operatorname{GL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) such that ρ′=A​ρ​A−1\rho^{\prime}=A\,\rho\,A^{-1}. Any Ad∘ρ\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho-invariant vector vρ∈𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)v_{\rho}\lx@nobreakspace\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) yields an Ad∘ρ′\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho^{\prime}-invariant vector vρ′=A​vρ​A−1v^{\prime}_{\rho}=A\,v_{\rho}\,A^{-1}, and the conjugation by AA induces an isomorphism

H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)→H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ′)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\to H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho^{\prime})

sending the basis {vρ⊗ℓ,vρ⊗m}\{v_{\rho}\otimes\ell,v_{\rho}\otimes m\} to {vρ′⊗ℓ,vρ′⊗m}\{v^{\prime}_{\rho}\varotimes\ell,v^{\prime}_{\rho}\varotimes m\} and the subspace 𝒵⁡(K,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(K,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) to 𝒵⁡(K,Ad∘ρ′)\mathcal{Z}(K,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho^{\prime}). Hence sK​(ρ)=sK​(ρ′)s_{K}(\rho)=s_{K}(\rho^{\prime}). ∎

Remark 3.7.

There exist pairs of reducible, non-conjugate representations with the same character. Indeed, let χ\chi be an arbitrary reducible character in X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}). Consider a representation ρ\rho of the form (λ⁡(γ)∗0λ−1​(γ))\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda(\gamma)&*\\ 0&\lambda^{-1}(\gamma)\end{smallmatrix}\right), where λ:π1​(MK)→ℂ∗\lambda\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\mathbb{C}^{*} is a group homomorphism, choosen such that χ⁡(ρ)=χ\chi(\rho)=\chi. Note that λ\lambda can further be written λ⁡(γ)=λφ⁡(γ)\lambda(\gamma)=\lambda^{\varphi(\gamma)} for some λ∈ℂ∗\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{*} and φ:π1​(MK)→ℤ\varphi:\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\mathbb{Z}. Hence the abelian representation ρλ\rho_{\lambda} defined in Eq. 4 has also character χ\chi, but is not conjugated in general to ρ\rho. It turns out that they can have different slope values.

For example, consider the right-handed trefoil knot TT in S3S^{3}. The character variety X⁡(MT)X(M_{T}) is the union of a line XredX^{\text{red}} and a conic XirrX^{\text{irr}} in the plane. The line contains only reducible characters, and any character in the conic is irreducible except the two intersection points Xred∩XirrX^{\text{red}}\cap X^{\text{irr}}. Let χ\chi be a point in Xred∩XirrX^{\text{red}}\cap X^{\text{irr}}. Since χ\chi is reducible, there exist λ∈ℂ∗\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^{*} such that the abelian representation ρλ\rho_{\lambda} has character χ\chi. By Lemma 3.5, one has sT​(ρλ)=0s_{T}(\rho_{\lambda})=0. However, we show in Example 3.19 that the slope defines a constant function on XirrX^{\text{irr}}, everywhere equal to −6-6.

3.3. Regularity and properties of the slope

We extend the slope to a rational function –locally a quotient of polynomials– on the character variety X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}).

There is a component Xred⊂X⁡(MK)X^{\text{red}}\subset X(M_{K}) of reducible characters only. By Remark 3.7 any character in XredX^{\text{red}} is the character of an abelian representation. Hence the slope is identically zero on XredX^{\text{red}}, see Lemma 3.5. Suppose now that X⊂X⁡(M)X\subset X(M) is an irreducible component containing an irreducible character.

Proposition 3.8.

Let X⊂X⁡(M)X\subset X(M) be an irreducible component which contains an irreducible character. The slope extends to a rational function on XX, still denoted sKs_{K}. Moreover, if χ∈X\chi\in X is a boundary-parabolic character then

(5) sK​(χ)=τ​(χ),s_{K}(\chi)=\tau(\chi),

where the modulus τ⁡(χ)∈ℂ\tau(\chi)\in\mathbb{C} is defined by taking the representative ρ\rho of χ\chi satisfying

ρ⁡(m)=(±110±1),ρ⁡(ℓ)=(±1τ⁡(χ)0±1).\rho(m)=\begin{pmatrix}\pm 1&1\\ 0&\pm 1\end{pmatrix},\quad\rho(\ell)=\begin{pmatrix}\pm 1&\tau(\chi)\\ 0&\pm 1\end{pmatrix}.
Remark 3.9.

If χ\chi is the character of an irreducible representation and lies at the intersection of several irreducible components, then the value of the slope at χ\chi is well-defined.

The rest of the section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 3.8. Lemma 3.10 asserts that the slope is a rational function in the neighborhood of any irreducible, non boundary-parabolic character. For boundary parabolic characters χ\chi, we define the slope by the relation in Eq. 5 and we show that the result is still a rational function on XX in Lemma 3.12.

Lemma 3.10.

Let χ0\chi_{0} an irreducible, non-boundary-parabolic character in XX. The slope is a rational function in a neighborhood of χ0\chi_{0} in XX.

Proof.

Let ρ0\rho_{0} in R⁡(MK)R(M_{K}) be a representation with character χ0\chi_{0}. By Lemma 3.4 one has H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)≃ℂ2H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\simeq\mathbb{C}^{2}. The set of complex lines

ℙ⁡(ρ)=ℙ⁡(H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ))\mathbb{P}(\rho)=\mathbb{P}(H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho))

is a complex algebraic variety isomorphic to ℂ​P1\mathbb{C}P^{1}. If ρ\rho and ρ′\rho^{\prime} are conjugate, then there is a natural algebraic isomorphism ℙ⁡(ρ)≃ℙ⁡(ρ′)\mathbb{P}(\rho)\simeq\mathbb{P}(\rho^{\prime}). It defines an algebraic ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration on a neighborhood of χρ0\chi_{\rho_{0}}, and for any χ\chi, the complex line 𝒵⁡(MK,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is an algebraic section of this fibration, independent of the choice of representation ρ\rho with character χ\chi.

It remains to show that the identification ℙ⁡(ρ)≃ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{P}(\rho)\simeq\mathbb{C}\mathbb{P}^{1} is algebraic, in other words, that the choice of the basis (vρ⊗ℓ,vρ⊗m)(v_{\rho}\otimes\ell,v_{\rho}\otimes m) depends algebraically on ρ\rho. Since ρ0\rho_{0} is not boundary-parabolic, we can shrink the chosen neighborhood so that no representation ρ\rho near ρ0\rho_{0} is boundary-parabolic. Then, since ρ∂\rho_{\partial} is conjugated to a diagonal representation, there is a unique Ad∘ρ∂\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{\partial}-invariant vector vρv_{\rho} with norm 11 in 𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}). This choice depends polynomially on the entries of the matrix Ad∘ρ⁡(m)\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho(m), and then the basis (vρ⊗ℓ,vρ⊗m)(v_{\rho}\otimes\ell,v_{\rho}\otimes m) depends algebraically on ρ\rho. ∎

We now consider the case of boundary-parabolic characters.

Lemma 3.11.

Let ρ0\rho_{0} be a boundary-parabolic representation whose character χρ0\chi_{\rho_{0}} lies in XX. Then ρ0\rho_{0} is irreducible, in particular ρ0​(m)≠±I2\rho_{0}(m)\neq\pm I_{2}.

Proof.

For ρ\rho reducible in XX, [5, 12] implies that ρ⁡(m)\rho(m) has eigenvalues λ,λ−1\lambda,\lambda^{-1} in ℂ\mathbb{C}, whose square is a root of the Alexander polynomial ΔMK​(t)\Delta_{M_{K}}(t), in particular λ≠±1\lambda\neq\pm 1, and ρ\rho is not boundary-parabolic. Now for irreducible ρ\rho, the image of any meridian must be different of I2I_{2}, since meridians generate the group π1​(MK)\pi_{1}(M_{K}). ∎

Lemma 3.12.

Let X⊂X⁡(M)X\subset X(M) be an irreducible component containing an irreducible character, and χ0∈X\chi_{0}\in X a boundary-parabolic character. Then the slope function sKs_{K} is rational in a neighborhood of χ0\chi_{0}.

Proof.

Suppose first that XX contains only boundary-parabolic characters. Any χ∈X\chi\in X is the character of a representation ρ\rho such that ρ⁡(m)=(±110±1)\rho(m)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\pm 1&1\\ 0&\pm 1\end{smallmatrix}\right). Hence χ↦τ⁡(χ)\chi\mapsto\tau(\chi) is rational.

Now we assume that XX contains a non boundary-parabolic character. By definition, boundary-parabolic characters form a Zariski closed subset of XX. By Lemma 3.10, the slope function is rational on the open, non-empty subset of XX consisting of non boundary-parabolic characters. By analytic continuation, it is enough to show that

limχ→χ0sK​(χ)=τ⁡(χ0).\lim_{\chi\to\chi_{0}}\lx@nobreakspace s_{K}(\chi)=\tau(\chi_{0}).

By Lemma 3.11 any boundary-parabolic representation ρ0\rho_{0} with character χ0\chi_{0} is irreducible. Moreover, since ρ0​(m)\rho_{0}(m) can not be trivial, we can chose such a ρ0\rho_{0} satifying

ρ0​(m)=(±110±1).\rho_{0}(m)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\pm 1&1\\ 0&\pm 1\end{smallmatrix}\right).

For any χ\chi close to χ0\chi_{0}, we chose similarly a representation ρ\rho with character χ\chi such that

ρ⁡(m)=(M10M−1),\rho(m)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}M&1\\ 0&M^{-1}\end{smallmatrix}\right),

with MM close to ±1\pm 1 in ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*}. For such ρ\rho, let vρ=(M−M−120M−1−M)v_{\rho}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}M-M^{-1}&2\\ 0&M^{-1}-M\end{smallmatrix}\right) be an Ad∘ρ∂\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{\partial}-invariant vector. The limit at ρ0\rho_{0} of vρv_{\rho} is the (Ad∘ρ0)∂(\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{0})_{\partial}-invariant vector vρ0=(0200)v_{\rho_{0}}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2\\ 0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right). However, a direct computation shows that vρ0⊗ℓv_{\rho_{0}}\otimes\ell and vρ0⊗mv_{\rho_{0}}\otimes m are linearly dependent in H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ0)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{0}), and we cannot compute the slope of the boundary parabolic representation ρ0\rho_{0} by means of Definition 3.2. Nevertheless, the subspace 𝒵⁡(K,Ad∘ρ0)\mathcal{Z}(K,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{0}) is one-dimensional by Lemma 3.4.

It implies that the map i∗:H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)→H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)i_{*}\colon H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\to H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) has rank one at any representation ρ\rho near ρ0\rho_{0}, and at ρ0\rho_{0} as well. In particular, for any ρ\rho near ρ0\rho_{0}, the slope can be computed as the ratio of i∗​(vρ⊗ℓ)i_{*}(v_{\rho}\otimes\ell) and i∗​(vρ⊗m)i_{*}(v_{\rho}\otimes m) in i∗​(H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ))i_{*}(H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)). vρ0⊗ℓ=τ⁡(χ0)​vρ0⊗mv_{\rho_{0}}\otimes\ell=\tau(\chi_{0})\,v_{\rho_{0}}\otimes m

holds in H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ0)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{0}). We end up this section with the following observation.

Proposition 3.13.

Let X⊂X⁡(M)X\subset X(M) be an irreducible component which contains a non boundary-parabolic representation. If ρ∈X\rho\in X is a real representation ρ:π1​(MK)→SL2⁡(ℝ)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) or ρ:π1​(MK)→SU⁡(2)\rho\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{SU}(2), then the slope is a real number in ℝ​ℙ1\mathbb{R}\mathbb{P}^{1}.

Proof.

First assume that ρ\rho is non-boundary-parabolic. If ρ\rho is real, denoting by Ad∘ρℝ\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{\mathbb{R}} the action of ρ\rho on the Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩2​(ℝ)\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) (resp. 𝔰​𝔲​(2)\mathfrak{su}(2)) of SL2⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) (resp. SU⁡(2)\operatorname{SU}(2)), then obviously the Lagrangian 𝒵⁡(MK,Ad∘ρ)⊂H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\subset H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is the complexification of the real Lagrangian 𝒵⁡(MK,Ad∘ρℝ)\mathcal{Z}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{\mathbb{R}}) in the real symplectic vector space H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρℝ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{\mathbb{R}}) and the slope of this real Lagrangian is the slope of its complexification, a real number. If ρ\rho is boundary-parabolic and re al, then it takes value into SL2⁡(ℝ)\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) and the proposition follows from the definition of the modulus τ\tau. ∎

3.4. Slope and Reidemeister torsion

In this section we show that the slope coincides with the "change of curve term" for the Reidemeister torsion as stated in Proposition 1.4.

If ρ\rho is an irreducible representation in X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}), we consider the torsion of the complex C∗​(MK,Ad∘ρ)C_{*}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) defined in Section 3.1. This complex is naturally based from a cell decomposition of MKM_{K} and a choice of a basis of 𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}), but not acyclic. The Reidemeister torsion is usually defined for acyclic complexes. In the case we are considering, one needs to make some additional choices to define it, namely a basis of each homology group H∗​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{*}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho).

According to [18], one can still define the Reidemeister torsion of the cellular complex C∗​(MK,Ad∘ρ)C_{*}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) for representations ρ\rho in R⁡(MK)R(M_{K}) such that H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) has dimension 11. For a given curve γ∈π1​(∂MK)\gamma\in\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K}), the representation ρ\rho is γ\gamma-regular if there exists a vector vρ∈𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)v_{\rho}\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) such that vρ⊗γv_{\rho}\otimes\gamma spans H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho). In this case, since there is a natural choice of a basis of H2​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{2}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho), the curve γ\gamma determines a homology basis of the complex C∗​(MK,Ad∘ρ)C_{*}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) and the torsion 𝕋MK,γ​(Ad∘ρ)∈ℂ∗\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\gamma}(\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\in\mathbb{C}^{*} is defined. Note that this torsion depends only on the conjugacy class of ρ\rho, as well as the property of being γ\gamma-regular.

Let X⊂X⁡(MK)X\subset X(M_{K}) the component containing χ\chi, the torsion function is the rational function

𝕋MK,γ:X→ℂ\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\gamma}\colon X\to\mathbb{C}

defined as the Reidemeister torsion of the complex C∗​(MK,Ad)C_{*}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}) if χ\chi is γ\gamma-regular, and by TMK,γ​(χ)=0T_{M_{K},\gamma}(\chi)=0 otherwise.

We start with the following lemma, which provides the genuine setting to define the Reidemeister torsion.

Lemma 3.14.

If XX has dimension one and contains the character of a scheme-smooth representation ρ\rho, then dimH1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)=1\dim H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)=1.

Proof.

The proof of Lemma 3.14 follows from the isomorphism between H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H^{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) and the Zariski tangent space of X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}) at ρ\rho, see [20, Theorem 1] . Scheme-smoothness implies that the Zariski tangent space is the actual tangent space, which is one-dimensional because XX is. ∎

Note that scheme-smoothness is a Zariski open condition.

It turns out that the character variety X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}) of a knot exterior is often one-dimensional. This is the case if the knot is small (if it does not contains a closed incompressible surface [7, Proposition 2.4]). This is also the case for any component X⊂X⁡(MK)X\subset X(M_{K}) containing the character of a lift of the holonomy representation ρ¯:π1​(MK)→PSL2⁡(ℂ)\overline{\rho}\colon\pi_{1}(M_{K})\to\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{C}), provided that the interior of MKM_{K} admits a hyperbolic structure.

The following proposition is the main result of this section.

Proposition 3.15.

Let X⊂X⁡(M)X\subset X(M) be an irreducible one-dimensional component which contains a scheme-smooth, non-boundary parabolic character. For all χ∈X\chi\in X the following holds

sK​(χ)=𝕋MK,ℓ​(χ)𝕋MK,m​(χ).s_{K}(\chi)=\frac{\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\ell}(\chi)}{\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},m}(\chi)}.

We provide two different proofs of this result: one uses the natural definition of the torsion while the other relies directly on some results on the torsion form proved by the first author in [2].

3.4.1. Torsion and chain complexes

This section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 3.15 by using the chain complex of MKM_{K}. The proof is very similar to [10, Theorem 3.21] or [10, Theorem 6.7]. We use the following technical lemma.

Lemma 3.16.

Let γ\gamma be a curve in π1​(∂MK)\pi_{1}(\partial M_{K}), and χ\chi be an irreducible γ\gamma-regular character in X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}). There exists a Zariski open neighborhood of χ\chi such that any character in this neighborhood is irreducible and γ\gamma-regular.

Proof.

Being irreducible is a Zariski open condition, see Eq. 2. The γ\gamma-regularity follows from lower semi-continuity of the rank of a linear map. Indeed the dimension of H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is upper semi-continuous. It is at least one (the dimension of XX) again because it is isomorphic to the Zariski tangent space hence it is locally constant equal to one. On the other hand, the rank of the linear map H1​(γ,Ad∘ρ)→H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\gamma,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\to H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) sending vρ⊗γv_{\rho}\otimes\gamma to itself is lower semi-continuous. It is at most one (the dimension of H1​(γ,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\gamma,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) and it cannot decrease on a neighborhood of χ\chi. We deduce that H1​(γ,Ad∘ρ)→H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\gamma,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\to H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is an isomorphism on a Zariski open subset. ∎

Proof of Proposition 3.15.

Let χ\chi be an irreducible, scheme-smooth, non boundary-parabolic character and let ρ\rho be a representation in R⁡(MK)R(M_{K}) with character χ\chi. We first assume that ρ\rho is ℓ\ell and mm-regular, that is for v∈𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)v\in\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) an Ad∘ρ∂\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho_{\partial}-invariant vector, both v⊗ℓv\otimes\ell and v⊗mv\otimes m provide a basis of H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho).

The calculation of the torsions 𝕋MK,ℓ​(χ)\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\ell}(\chi) and 𝕋MK,m​(χ)\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},m}(\chi) involves different choices of homology basis of C∗​(MK,Ad∘ρ)C_{*}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho). By [18, Proposition 3.18], the bases of H2​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{2}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) are determined by the fundamental class of H2​(∂MK,ℂ)H_{2}(\partial M_{K};\mathbb{C}) and can be choosen to be the same. Hence, if b1b_{1} is a basis of im(∂1)\mathrm{im}(\partial_{1}), the ratio of torsions corresponding to the choice of mm or of ℓ\ell is reduced to

𝕋MK,ℓ​(χ)𝕋MK,m​(χ)=det(b1⊕(v⊗ℓ),c1)det(b1⊕(v⊗m),c1).\frac{\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},\ell}(\chi)}{\mathbb{T}_{M_{K},m}(\chi)}=\frac{\det(b_{1}\oplus(v\otimes\ell),c_{1})}{\det(b_{1}\oplus(v\otimes m),c_{1})}.

In parallel, consider the affine equation in C1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)C_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho):

y​b1+x​v⊗m=v⊗ℓ,y\,b_{1}+x\,v\otimes m=v\otimes\ell,

with at least a solution y=0y=0 and x=sK​(ρ)x=s_{K}(\rho). The Cramer determinants expressed in the common basis c1c_{1} show that sK​(ρ)s_{K}(\rho) coincides with the ratio of torsions.

If there exists a character in XX which is ℓ\ell-regular and a character in XX which is mm-regular, then Proposition 3.15 holds on the whole component XX by Lemma 3.16.

Assume that XX contains only characters that are not (say) ℓ\ell-regular. Since the map H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)→H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\to H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is not trivial (by Lemma 3.4), it is onto on a Zariski open subset U∈XU\in X, again because H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) has dimension one generically. Thus all characters in UU must be mm-regular, and it follows from the definition that the slope and the quotient of torsions are identically zero on XX. A similar argument works replacing ℓ\ell by mm and zero by infinity. ∎

3.4.2. The torsion form

In this paragraph, we present an alternative proof of Proposition 3.15. We follow a slightly different point of view on the torsion, as a volume form on the character variety. The following lemma asserts that the cotangent space of the character variety [20, Section 8] is isomorphic to the first Ad∘ρ\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho-twisted homology group.

Lemma 3.17.

Let χ\chi be an irreducible character in X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}), and a representation ρ\rho with character χ\chi. Let Tχ∗​X​(MK)T^{*}_{\chi}X(M_{K}) be the Zariski tangent space of X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}) at χ\chi. There is a natural isomorphism

H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)≃Tχ∗​X​(MK).H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\simeq T^{*}_{\chi}X(M_{K}).

Moreover, if χ\chi is not boundary-parabolic, then

H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)≃Tr⁡(χ)∗​X​(∂MK).H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\simeq T^{*}_{r(\chi)}X(\partial M_{K}).

The proof of Lemma 3.17 follows from [20, Theorem 1]. Note that through the isomorphim, the space 𝒵⁡(K,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(K,\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) is the Zariski conormal bundle of r⁡(X⁡(MK))r(X(M_{K})) in X⁡(∂MK)X(\partial M_{K}).

If X⊂X⁡(MK)X\subset X(M_{K}) is a one-dimensional component of the character variety which contains a scheme-smooth character, the first author proved in [2, Proposition 5.1] that the torsion form can be written as

(6) tor⁡(MK)=1𝕋MK,ℓ​r∗​(d​LL)=1𝕋MK,m​r∗​(d​MM)\operatorname{tor}(M_{K})=\frac{1}{{\mathbb{T}}_{M_{K},\ell}}r^{*}\left(\frac{dL}{L}\right)=\frac{1}{{\mathbb{T}}_{M_{K},m}}r^{*}\left(\frac{dM}{M}\right)

where r∗r^{*} is the cotangent map

r∗:T∗​X​(∂MK)→T∗​X​(MK).r^{*}\colon T^{*}X(\partial M_{K})\to T^{*}X(M_{K}).
Proof of Proposition 3.15.

By Eq. 6, the ratio of torsions can be written as

𝕋MK,ℓ𝕋MK,m=r∗​(d​L/L)r∗​(d​M/M).\frac{{\mathbb{T}}_{M_{K},\ell}}{{\mathbb{T}}_{M_{K},m}}=\frac{r^{*}(dL/L)}{r^{*}(dM/M)}.

If χ\chi is a non boundary-parabolic character, the character variety X⁡(∂MK)X(\partial M_{K}) is diffeomorphic to (ℂ∗)2(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2} in a neighborhood of r⁡(χ)r(\chi). A local chart of X⁡(∂MK)X(\partial M_{K}) is given by taking 𝔩,𝔪∈ℂ\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{m}\in\mathbb{C} satisfying exp⁡𝔩=L\exp\mathfrak{l}=L and exp⁡𝔪=M\exp\mathfrak{m}=M. The latter ratio of torsions can be written

𝕋MK,ℓ𝕋MK,m=r∗​(d​𝔩)r∗​(d​𝔪).\frac{{\mathbb{T}}_{M_{K},\ell}}{{\mathbb{T}}_{M_{K},m}}=\frac{r^{*}(d\,\mathfrak{l})}{r^{*}(d\,\mathfrak{m})}.

Lemma 3.17 implies that the cotangent map r∗:Tr⁡(χ)∗​X​(∂MK)→Tχ∗​X​(MK)r^{*}\colon T^{*}_{r(\chi)}X(\partial M_{K})\to T^{*}_{\chi}X(M_{K}) coincides with the homomorphism in homology H1​(∂MK,Ad∘ρ)→H1​(MK,Ad∘ρ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho)\to H_{1}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho), thus by Lemma 3.4 the range of the map r∗r^{*} is one-dimensional, and the images of the elements d​𝔩,d​𝔪d\,\mathfrak{l},d\,\mathfrak{m} are colinear. It turns out that the ratio r∗​(d​𝔩)r∗​(d​𝔪)\frac{r^{*}(d\,\mathfrak{l})}{r^{*}(d\,\mathfrak{m})} coincides with the slope by its very definition.

Finally, the formula extends to the whole XX since irreducible, non boundary-parabolic character are Zariski dense in XX. ∎

4. Slope and A-polynomial

In this section, we express the slope function in terms of the A-polynomial of the knot. As mentioned in Section 2.3, r⁡(X)r(X) might have 00-dimensional components but they are omitted in the definition of the A-polynomial.

Theorem 4.1.

Let X⊂X⁡(MK)X\subset X(M_{K}) be an irreducible component such that r⁡(X)r(X) has dimension 11. For all χ∈X\chi\in X with r⁡(χ)=(L,M)r(\chi)=(L,M), the following holds

sK(χ)=−ML⋅∂MA⁡(L,M)∂LA⁡(L,M),s_{K}(\chi)=-\frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{\partial_{M}A(L,M)}{\partial_{L}A(L,M)},

where A⁡(L,M)=AK​(L,M)A(L,M)=A_{K}(L,M) and ∂L\partial_{L} and ∂M\partial_{M} are the partial derivatives.

Remark 4.2.

Combining Proposition 3.15 with [18, Corollaire 4.9], the result of Theorem 4.1 follows directly, up to sign, in the case where XX has itself dimension 11. We resolve those two issues. Moreover Theorem 4.1 does not require the characters in XX to be scheme-reduced, and the factors of the A-polynomial might have multiplicities greater than 11.

Proof.

From Lemma 3.17 it follows that the Lagrangian 𝒵⁡(MK,Ad∘ρ)\mathcal{Z}(M_{K},\operatorname{Ad}\circ\rho) generically identifies with the Zariski conormal bundle of r⁡(X⁡(MK))r(X(M_{K})) in X⁡(∂MK)X(\partial M_{K}). Picking local coordinates 𝔩=log⁡L,𝔪=log⁡M\mathfrak{l}=\log L,\mathfrak{m}=\log M around r⁡(χ)r(\chi), the kernel of the cotangent map is generated by

d​A​(e𝔩,e𝔪)=∂𝔩A⁡(e𝔩,e𝔪)​d​𝔩+∂𝔪A⁡(e𝔩,e𝔪)​d​𝔪dA(e^{\mathfrak{l}},e^{\mathfrak{m}})=\partial_{\mathfrak{l}}A(e^{\mathfrak{l}},e^{\mathfrak{m}})d\mathfrak{l}+\partial_{\mathfrak{m}}A(e^{\mathfrak{l}},e^{\mathfrak{m}})d\mathfrak{m}

in ℂ2=⟨d​𝔩,d​𝔪⟩\mathbb{C}^{2}=\langle d\mathfrak{l},d\mathfrak{m}\rangle. Using the chain rule, we obtain that it is generated by the vector

(L​∂A⁡(M,L)∂L,M​∂A⁡(M,L)∂M)\left(L\frac{\partial A(M,L)}{\partial L},M\frac{\partial A(M,L)}{\partial M}\right)

and the proposition follows. ∎

Remark 4.3.

Let TT be the right-handed trefoil knot, with AT​(L,M)=1+L​M6A_{T}(L,M)=1+LM^{6}. Theorem 4.1 gives

sT=−ML⋅6​M5​LM6=−6.s_{T}=-\frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{6M^{5}L}{M^{6}}=-6.

Compare to Example 3.19.

5. The slope at an ideal point

In this section we prove Theorem 1.5. The context of this result is the work of Culler–Shalen (see for instance [19]) which associates incompressible surfaces in MKM_{K} to ideal points of curves of X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}).

Let X⊂X⁡(MK)X\subset X(M_{K}) be an irreducible component whose image r⁡(X)=Yr(X)=Y is a curve in X⁡(∂MK)X(\partial M_{K}), defined as the zero locus of an irreducible factor PP of AK​(L,M)A_{K}(L,M). Its function ring is usually denoted by ℂ⁡[Y]=ℂ⁡[L,M]/(P)\mathbb{C}[Y]=\mathbb{C}[L,M]/(P), and its function field is ℂ⁡(Y)=Frac⁡(ℂ⁡[Y])\mathbb{C}(Y)=\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb{C}[Y]).

To any point yy in YY one can associate a discrete valuation vv on the multiplicative group ℂ​(Y)∗\mathbb{C}(Y)^{*} in the field ℂ⁡(Y)\mathbb{C}(Y) of rational functions on YY. A discrete valuation v:ℂ​(Y)∗→ℤv\colon\mathbb{C}(Y)^{*}\to\mathbb{Z} is a group epimorphism satisfying v⁡(f+g)≥min⁡(v⁡(f),v⁡(g))v(f+g)\geq\min(v(f),v(g)). The valuation associated to a smooth point yy is simply the map

f↦vy​(f)=ordy⁡ff\mapsto v_{y}(f)=\operatorname{ord}_{y}f

given the vanishing order of ff at the point yy. More generally, the smooth projective model Y¯\overline{Y} of YY is smooth compact curve birational to YY, canonically defined up to isomorphism, and the points of Y¯\overline{Y} are bijectively associated to discrete valuations on the function field ℂ⁡(Y)≃ℂ⁡(Y¯)\mathbb{C}(Y)\simeq\mathbb{C}(\overline{Y}).

An ideal point yy of YY is a point added "at infinity" in the smooth projective model Y¯\overline{Y}, it corresponds to a valuation vyv_{y} on ℂ⁡(Y)\mathbb{C}(Y) such that not every regular function f∈ℂ⁡[Y]f\in\mathbb{C}[Y] has non-negative valuation vy​(f)v_{y}(f). In other words, some regular functions (at least one) should have poles at yy.

In [9], Marc Culler and Peter Shalen gave a procedure to construct an incompressible surface Σ\Sigma in MKM_{K} from the data of an ideal point xx in a subcurve CC of X⁡(MK)X(M_{K}) together with the valuation vx:ℂ​(C)∗→ℤv_{x}\lx@nobreakspace\colon\mathbb{C}(C)^{*}\to\mathbb{Z}. Not any ideal point x∈X⁡(MK)x\in X(M_{K}) yields an ideal point y=r⁡(x)∈X⁡(∂MK)y=r(x)\in X(\partial M_{K}).

In this special case, the ideal point yy in YY gives an incompressible surface in MKM_{K} of a particular kind: as observed in [7, Proposition 3.1], the incompressible surface Σ\Sigma must have non-empty boundary ∂Σ⊂∂MK\partial\Sigma\subset\partial M_{K}. The curve ∂Σ\partial\Sigma is a finite union of parallel circles in ∂MK\partial M_{K} and uniquely determines a boundary slope in ℚ∪{∞}\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}: the slope of a​ℓ+b​ma\ell+bm in H1​(∂MK,ℤ)H_{1}(\partial M_{K};\mathbb{Z}) is the rational number ba\frac{b}{a}.

On the other hand, the Newton polygon of AK​(L,M)=∑i,jai,j​Li​MjA_{K}(L,M)=\sum_{i,j}a_{i,j}L^{i}M^{j} is the convex hull in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} of the points {(i,j)∈ℤ2∣ai,j≠0}\{(i,j)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\mid a_{i,j}\neq 0\}. It is a convex polygon of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with integral vertices, whose sides have a slope in ℚ∪{∞}\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}. In [7], Culler, Cooper, Gillet, Long and Shalen proved the following result:

Theorem 5.1.

[7, Theorem 3.4] The slopes of the sides of the Newton polygon of the AA-polynomial AK​(L,M)A_{K}(L,M) are boundary slopes of incompressible surfaces in MKM_{K} which correspond to ideal points of one-dimensional components of r∗​(X⁡(MK))r^{*}(X(M_{K})) in X⁡(∂MK)X(\partial M_{K}).

Our next statement (Theorem 1.5 in the introduction) states that the slope invariant studied in this paper coincides with the slopes of [7] at ideal points.

Theorem 5.2.

Let yy be an ideal point in a one-dimensional component YY of the AA-polynomial. Then the value of the slope function at the ideal point yy equals minus the boundary slope of an incompressible surface corresponding to yy or minus the slope of the corresponding side of the Newton polygon of the AA-polynomial.

Proof.

The coordinate functions L,ML,M define rational functions on YY, in particular their valuations vy​(L)v_{y}(L) and vy​(M)v_{y}(M) are well-defined. Since yy is an ideal point and L,ML,M generate the coordinate ring ℂ⁡[Y]\mathbb{C}[Y] of the curve YY, at least one of this valuation must be negative, and at least one of these coordinate functions must have a pole at yy.

Claim.

The value of sKs_{K} at the ideal point yy is vy​(L)vy​(M)\frac{v_{y}(L)}{v_{y}(M)}.

Proof of the claim.

From the proof of Proposition 3.15, we deduce that the value of the slope at yy is given by

sK​(y)=lim(L,M)→yr∗​(d​L/L)r∗​(d​M/M).s_{K}(y)=\lim_{(L,M)\to y}\frac{r^{*}(dL/L)}{r^{*}(dM/M)}.

The following argument is an algebraic analogue of taking Taylor expansion of the functions LL and MM around the ideal point yy. We pick tt a local coordinate around yy. It is characterized by vy​(t)=1v_{y}(t)=1, and we can write

L=u1​tvy​(L)L=u_{1}t^{v_{y}(L)}

for u1∈ℂ⁡(Y),vy​(u1)=0u_{1}\in\mathbb{C}(Y),v_{y}(u_{1})=0, and similarly

M=u2​tvy​(M)M=u_{2}t^{v_{y}(M)}

for u2∈ℂ⁡(Y),vy​(u2)=0u_{2}\in\mathbb{C}(Y),v_{y}(u_{2})=0. Moreover, near yy it follows that

r∗​(d​L/L)r∗​(d​M/M)=vy​(L)/tvy​(M)/t=vy​(L)vy​(M)\frac{r^{*}(dL/L)}{r^{*}(dM/M)}=\frac{v_{y}(L)/t}{v_{y}(M)/t}=\frac{v_{y}(L)}{v_{y}(M)}

and the claim follows. ∎

Now Theorem 1.5 follows directly from the claim, because it is proven in [7, Proposition 3.1] that the quantity −vy​(L)vy​(M)-\frac{v_{y}(L)}{v_{y}(M)} is the boundary slope of an incompressible surface corresponding to yy. ∎
